definitions.text: Information handling is the process of collecting, organizing, summarizing, analyzing and interpreting numerical data.
So, the collection of meaningful information in the form of facts and numerical figures is known as data.

It can take only some specific values. whole numbers are used to write discrete data. e.g., number of books sold by a shopkeeper, number of patients visited a hospital in a week etc. This data is only obtained by counting.

It can take every possible value in a given interval. Decimal numbers are used to write continuous data. The data is only obtained by measuring e.g., the mass of students in class i.e., 28.5 kg, 26.5 kg, 27.5 kg etc.
Data which is not arranged in any systematic order (groups or classes) is called ungrouped data.
If we arrange the above given data in groups or classes, then it is called grouped data.
Range is the difference between the greatest value and the smallest value i.e., Range = Xₘₐₓ − Xₘᵢₙ
The number of times a value occurs in a data is called the frequency of that value. It is denoted by “f”.

This is a graph of adjacent rectangles constructed on xy plane. A histogram is similar to bar graph but it is constructed for a frequency distribution. In a histogram, the values of the data (classes) are represented along the horizontal axis and the frequencies are shown by bars perpendicular to the horizontal axis. Bars of equal width are used to represent individual classes of frequency table.

A frequency polygon is a closed geometrical figure used to display a frequency distribution graphically. A line graph of a frequency distribution is known as frequency polygon in which frequencies are plotted against their midpoints.
Midpoint is the average value of the lower and upper class limits. Midpoint is also known as class mark.
The measure that gives the centre of the data is called measure of central tendency. Therefore, measure of central tendency is used to find out the middle or central value of a data set.
It is defined as a value of variable which is obtained by dividing the sum of all the values (observations) by their number of observations.

Median is the middle most value in an arranged (ascending or descending order) data set. Median is the value which divides the data into two equal parts i.e., 50% data is before the median and 50% data after it. Median is denoted by X̃.
In a data the values (observation) which appears or occurs most often is called mode of the data. It is the most common value. Mode is denoted by X̂.

Arithmetic Mean is used when all the observations are given equal importance / weight but there are certain situations in which the different observations get different weights. In this situation, weighted mean denoted by X̄_w is preferred.

fullMarks: For a frequency table, show the range and class-size calculation first; then make clear columns for class limits, tally marks, frequency and class boundaries when required.
For a histogram, label both axes, mark class boundaries on the horizontal axis, use a stated scale and draw adjoining rectangles. For unequal class widths, calculate and use adjusted frequencies.
For a frequency polygon, show the midpoint calculation, plot each midpoint against its frequency, join the points with straight lines and extend both ends to the x-axis.
For a grouped mean, include columns for midpoint x and fx (or deviation D and fD); show Σf and Σfx (or ΣfD) before substituting into the formula.
For an ungrouped median, arrange all values in ascending or descending order and state the observation position before giving the answer. For even n, average the two middle observations.
For a grouped median, show the cumulative-frequency column, identify the median class and state ℓ, h, f, n and c before substitution.
For a grouped mode, identify the modal class and clearly state ℓ, h, fₘ, f₁ and f₂. Finish with a sentence giving the answer and its units when the data has units.
mistakes: Using class limits instead of class boundaries on a histogram when the classes are written in inclusive form. Find the boundaries first, such as 24–28 becoming 23.5–28.5.
Drawing gaps between histogram bars. Histogram rectangles for continuous classes must touch.
Using the original frequencies as rectangle heights for unequal-width classes. Divide each frequency by its class width to get the adjusted frequency.
Plotting class limits instead of midpoints for a frequency polygon. Calculate and plot the midpoint of every class.
Finding the median before arranging raw data, or choosing the wrong middle position. Arrange the values first and then use the odd- or even-number formula.
Using the wrong cumulative frequency in the grouped-median formula. Use c as the cumulative frequency before the median class, not the cumulative frequency of that class.
Mixing up the modal-class frequency and its neighbouring frequencies. Use fₘ for the modal class, f₁ for the class before it and f₂ for the class after it.

shortTheory.question: Define frequency distribution.
shortTheory.answer: A distribution or table that represents classes or groups along with their respective class frequencies is called frequency distribution. In other words, the various items of data are classified into certain groups or classes and the number of items lying in each group or class is put against that group or class. The data organised and summarized in this way is known as frequency distribution.
